title: Week 7
text:
Pros / Cons (cont.)








Feature
ARIMA
Prophet




Model complexity
Needs careful tuning (p,d,q) and domain expertise
Defaults work well; limited tuning needed


Holiday effects
Must be encoded manually
Easy to include holidays/events


Multivariate support
Basic ARIMA doesn’t support exogenous variables easily (need ARIMAX)
Supports external regressors with add_regressor()


Non-linear trends
Poor performance with structural breaks or non-linear growth
Handles changepoints and logistic growth models well


Seasonality limits
SARIMA handles only one seasonal period well
Built-in multiple seasonal components (e.g., daily, weekly, yearly)



TL;DR

Use ARIMA for a classical, statistical model with deep customization: when you’re comfortable making your data stationary.
Use Prophet for a fast, robust, intuitive model: when data has strong seasonal effects, irregular events, or missing values.

title: Week 7
section: Bringing It Home: Forecasting Streamflow at Lees Ferry
text:
Bringing It Home: Forecasting Streamflow at Lees Ferry
In Lab 1 you built an analytical pipeline for the Colorado River: pulling 44 years of daily discharge from USGS NWIS, normalizing by drainage area, detecting low-flow threshold exceedances, and modeling the upstream-downstream relationship between Glenwood Springs and Lees Ferry.
Now we apply everything from this lecture to that same data:

Pull daily discharge at Lees Ferry with dataRetrieval
Convert to a monthly time series (the natural forecasting granularity)
Fit multiple models with modeltime: ARIMA, Prophet, ETS
Evaluate three rounds of model refinement — and learn from each failure

Lees Ferry is the Colorado River Compact’s primary accounting point. Forecasting flow here has direct operational consequences for 40 million people across 7 states.

title: Week 7
text:
Step 1: Pull Data with dataRetrieval

library(dataRetrieval)
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(modeltime)
library(tidymodels)
library(timetk)

# Lees Ferry: the Compact's accounting point (same gage as Lab 1)
lees_daily <- readNWISdv(
  siteNumbers = "09380000",
  parameterCd = "00060",        # discharge, cfs
  startDate   = "1980-01-01",
  endDate     = "2023-12-31"
) |>
  renameNWISColumns() |>
  select(Date, Flow)

glimpse(lees_daily)
#> Rows: 16,071
#> Columns: 2
#> $ Date <date> 1980-01-01, 1980-01-02, 1980-01-03, 1980-01-04, 1980-01-05, 1980…
#> $ Flow <dbl> 2650, 8560, 9480, 10200, 10700, 6670, 12900, 14400, 16500, 7910, …

title: Week 7
text:
Step 2: Aggregate to Monthly
Daily data is noisy and computationally heavy for forecasting. Monthly mean discharge captures the hydrologically meaningful signal: the seasonal snowmelt cycle: while filtering short-term noise.






Note


Mean vs. sum? For forecasting we use mean(Flow): it normalizes for months with different lengths and focuses on flow intensity. For operational water accounting (e.g., Compact compliance), use sum(Flow) to get total volume delivered. Know which question you’re answering before you aggregate.




lees_monthly <- lees_daily |>
  mutate(date = floor_date(Date, "month")) |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(flow = mean(Flow, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

lees_monthly
#> # A tibble: 528 × 2
#>    date         flow
#>    <date>      <dbl>
#>  1 1980-01-01  9825.
#>  2 1980-02-01 10696.
#>  3 1980-03-01  9851.
#>  4 1980-04-01 14505.
#>  5 1980-05-01 13749.
#>  6 1980-06-01 24739.
#>  7 1980-07-01 25777.
#>  8 1980-08-01 20794.
#>  9 1980-09-01 16490 
#> 10 1980-10-01 12637.
#> # ℹ 518 more rows

title: Week 7
text:
Step 3: Visualize the Series

lees_monthly |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = flow)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.15, color = "darkred", se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Monthly Mean Discharge: Lees Ferry, AZ",
       subtitle = "USGS 09380000 | 1980–2023",
       x = NULL, y = "Discharge (cfs)") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Week 7
text:
What do you see?



Trend: A long-term decline post-2000: the megadrought fingerprint
Seasonality: Annual snowmelt pulse peaking May–June, trough in autumn
Anomalies: 2011 and 2023 stand out as exceptional wet years (La Niña recovery / atmospheric rivers)


This series has all three components from decomposition:

A non-stationary trend (declining)
Strong seasonality (monthly cycle)
Structured remainder (ENSO-driven anomalies)

This is exactly the kind of series where modeltime shines.

title: Week 7
text:
Step 4: Train / Test Split
Hold out the last 5 years (2019–2023) as the test set — matching the assess = "60 months" logic from the CO₂ example.

splits <- time_series_split(
  lees_monthly,
  date_var   = date,
  assess     = "60 months",
  cumulative = TRUE
)

training(splits) |> tail(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   date         flow
#>   <date>      <dbl>
#> 1 2018-10-01 10576.
#> 2 2018-11-01 11236 
#> 3 2018-12-01 12100
testing(splits)  |> head(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   date         flow
#>   <date>      <dbl>
#> 1 2019-01-01 13252.
#> 2 2019-02-01 13350 
#> 3 2019-03-01 12971.

title: Week 7
text:
Step 5: Specify Models

mods <- list(
  # Classical: let auto.arima find the best seasonal ARIMA
  arima_reg() |> set_engine("auto_arima"),

  # ARIMA + XGBoost residual boosting
  arima_boost(min_n = 2, learn_rate = 0.015) |>
    set_engine("auto_arima_xgboost"),

  # Facebook Prophet — handles the trend break around 2000 well
  prophet_reg(seasonality_yearly = TRUE) |> set_engine("prophet"),

  # Exponential smoothing — strong baseline for seasonal data
  exp_smoothing() |> set_engine("ets")
)

title: Week 7
text:
Step 6: Fit & Calibrate

models <- map(mods, ~ fit(.x, flow ~ date, data = training(splits)))

models_tbl <- as_modeltime_table(models)

calibration_tbl <- modeltime_calibrate(models_tbl, testing(splits), quiet = FALSE)

Step 8: Forecast Forward 5 Years

fc <- calibration_tbl |>
  modeltime_forecast(h = "5 years", actual_data = lees_monthly)

fc |>
  filter(.key == "actual") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .index, y = .value)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = filter(fc, .key == "prediction"),
            aes(color = .model_desc)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = filter(fc, .key == "prediction"),
              aes(ymin = .conf_lo, ymax = .conf_hi, fill = .model_desc),
              alpha = 0.1) +

  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(title = "Lees Ferry 5-Year Discharge Forecast",
       x = NULL, y = "Monthly Mean Discharge (cfs)",
       color = "Model", fill = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Week 7
section: What Does the Forecast Tell Us?
text:
What Does the Forecast Tell Us?


What the model gets right:

The seasonal cycle: spring pulse, summer drawdown, winter baseflow — the timing is reliable
The general magnitude range: models trained on post-2000 data capture the modern low-flow regime
Uncertainty grows appropriately beyond 12–18 months — honest about what it doesn’t know


What it cannot do:

Anticipate wet-year spikes (2023-type events) without a leading SWE signal
Distinguish drought persistence from mean reversion
Outperform “repeat last year” on inter-annual magnitude

What would actually help: April 1 SWE at key basins, reservoir storage anomaly, PDO/ENSO phase — leading indicators, not concurrent observations. This is what USBR’s operational ESP system uses.






Tip


In Lab 6 you’ll add exactly this kind of outside information — GridMET climate covariates (precipitation, temperature, solar radiation) and MACA future projections — to your Poudre River forecast. That’s the missing ingredient here.

title: Week 7
text:
Connecting Back to Lab 1
In Lab 1 you:

Pulled this exact gage with readNWISdv() and renameNWISColumns()
Computed the 7-day rolling mean and flagged below-threshold days
Built a water-year bar chart showing the post-2000 decline
Fit a simple log-log linear model from Glenwood Springs → Lees Ferry

Today you extended that pipeline to time series forecasting:







Lab 1 skill

Same: data foundation unchanged

→ decompose() / stl() for formal decomposition

→ Trend + remainder components

→ Glenwood as exogenous regressor in ARIMAX / Prophet

→ modeltime time series model with flow ~ date + glenwood


Annual bar chart
→ Calibrated 5-year probabilistic forecast

Key takeaways:

title: Week 7
text:
Reading the Forecast Chart
The grey line is the full historical record (1980–2023). The coloured lines + ribbons are the 5-year forward forecast.
Why does the series start so high in 1980–1984?
The early 1980s were an exceptional period in the Upper Colorado Basin:

Record snowpack across the Rockies (1982–1984 La Niña cluster)
Glen Canyon Dam spillway capacity nearly exceeded in 1983 — the highest recorded inflow since the dam closed
The ~55,000 cfs peak in 1984 is the single largest monthly mean in the 44-year record

This is not an artifact or error — it is genuine signal. It also illustrates why models trained on post-2000 data alone would have no way to anticipate such extremes: the training distribution simply doesn’t include them.
The forecast ribbons at the right edge represent model uncertainty — wider = less confident. All models anchor near the recent 10,000–12,000 cfs regime, reflecting the post-2000 megadrought baseline.

title: Week 7
section: Why All MASE > 1? The Training Data Problem
text:
Why All MASE > 1? The Training Data Problem
All models were trained on 1980–2023 — but the 1980s high-flow regime is structurally different from the post-2000 drought world:



The 1984 peak (~55,000 cfs) is 5× the current typical flow
Training a model on this data teaches it a world that no longer exists
Every model wastes capacity “learning” the pre-2000 regime it will never need to forecast












Fix #1: Restrict training to the post-2000 regime that actually represents today’s conditions.

title: Week 7
text:
Round 1: Restrict to Post-2000 Regime

lees_modern <- lees_monthly |>
  filter(date >= "2000-01-01")

splits_modern <- time_series_split(
  lees_modern,
  date_var   = date,
  assess     = "60 months",
  cumulative = TRUE
)

Same models, same workflow: only the training window changes:

mods <- list(
  arima_reg()                                        |> set_engine("auto_arima"),
  arima_boost(min_n = 2, learn_rate = 0.015)         |> set_engine("auto_arima_xgboost"),
  prophet_reg(seasonality_yearly = TRUE)             |> set_engine("prophet"),
  exp_smoothing()                                    |> set_engine("ets")
)

models_v1 <- map(mods, ~ fit(.x, flow ~ date, data = training(splits_modern)))

cal_v1 <- as_modeltime_table(models_v1) |>
  modeltime_calibrate(testing(splits_modern), quiet = FALSE)

title: Week 7
text:
Round 1: Results

modeltime_accuracy(cal_v1) |>
  arrange(mase) |>
  select(.model_desc, mae, mape, mase, rmse, rsq)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   .model_desc                                  mae  mape  mase  rmse   rsq
#>   <chr>                                      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 ETS(M,N,M)                                 1767.  16.2  1.48 2293. 0.217
#> 2 PROPHET                                    1882.  17.5  1.58 2405. 0.222
#> 3 ARIMA(2,0,1)(1,0,1)[12] WITH NON-ZERO MEAN 1897.  18.0  1.59 2405. 0.204
#> 4 ARIMA(1,0,1)(2,0,0)[12] WITH NON-ZERO MEAN 1919.  18.4  1.61 2471. 0.200


MASE of 1.48–1.61 means all four models are worse than the naïve seasonal benchmark — simply repeating last year’s value would outperform every model here. Restricting to post-2000 data did not help; it may have made things worse by reducing the training set size, giving the models less signal to learn the seasonal pattern.
Two things MASE > 1 tells us:

Time structure alone (AR, MA, seasonal lags) is insufficient — the series has variance driven by physical drivers the model cannot see
The benchmark (last year’s value) is hard to beat because the seasonal cycle is highly stable; errors come from inter-annual variability in snowpack magnitude, not timing

Round 1 verdict: MASE got worse (1.48–1.61). Hypothesis rejected — restricting the window removed signal, not noise. New hypothesis: models need physical information about upstream conditions to anticipate inter-annual variability.

title: Week 7
Week 7
text:
Round 2: Split with Regressor
The regressor must be present in both training and the future forecast window. For an h-step ahead forecast we use the known test-period Glenwood values as the “future” regressor: valid because upstream data is available in near real-time from NWIS.

splits_reg <- time_series_split(
  lees_reg,
  date_var   = date,
  assess     = "60 months",
  cumulative = TRUE
)

train_reg <- training(splits_reg)
test_reg  <- testing(splits_reg)

title: Week 7
text:
Round 2: Models with Regressor
Only models that accept xreg / external regressors participate. Prophet and ARIMA both support this natively in modeltime:

mods_reg <- list(
  # ARIMA with exogenous regressor (ARIMAX)
  arima_reg() |> set_engine("auto_arima"),

  # Prophet with Glenwood as an additive regressor
  prophet_reg(seasonality_yearly = TRUE) |> set_engine("prophet"),

  # Boosted ARIMA: XGBoost picks up nonlinear upstream signal
  arima_boost(min_n = 2, learn_rate = 0.015) |>
    set_engine("auto_arima_xgboost")
)

models_v2 <- map(mods_reg, ~ fit(.x, flow ~ date + glenwood, data = train_reg))

cal_v2 <- as_modeltime_table(models_v2) |>
  modeltime_calibrate(test_reg, quiet = FALSE)

title: Week 7
text:
Round 2: Results

modeltime_accuracy(cal_v2) |>
  arrange(mase) |>
  select(.model_desc, mae, mape, mase, rmse, rsq)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   .model_desc                                        mae  mape  mase  rmse   rsq
#>   <chr>                                            <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 REGRESSION WITH ARIMA(1,0,1)(2,0,0)[12] ERRORS   1857.  17.9  1.56 2401. 0.320
#> 2 ARIMA(2,0,1)(1,0,1)[12] WITH NON-ZERO MEAN W/ X… 1859.  17.7  1.56 2375. 0.232
#> 3 PROPHET W/ REGRESSORS                            2104.  20.1  1.76 2546. 0.315


MASE of 1.56–1.76 — still worse than naïve. Adding the upstream Glenwood regressor moved the needle marginally (ARIMA dropped from ~1.59 to 1.56) but did not solve the problem. Prophet with regressors actually got worse (1.76).
Why didn’t it work?

A single upstream gage captures flow volume but not its timing or source (snowmelt vs. rain-on-snow vs. baseflow)
The regressor is contemporaneous — we’re using current Glenwood flow to predict current Lees Ferry flow, which is nearly circular at monthly resolution
The naïve benchmark (repeat last year) is genuinely hard to beat on a highly seasonal series with stable timing but variable magnitude

title: Week 7
text:
Comparing All Three Rounds

bind_rows(
  modeltime_accuracy(cal_v0) |> mutate(round = "v0: Full record 1980–2023 (baseline)"),
  modeltime_accuracy(cal_v1) |> mutate(round = "v1: Post-2000 only"),
  modeltime_accuracy(cal_v2) |> mutate(round = "v2: Post-2000 + upstream regressor")
) |>
  group_by(round) |>
  slice_min(mase, n = 1) |>
  select(round, .model_desc, mae, mase, rmse, rsq) |>
  arrange(mase)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#> # Groups:   round [3]
#>   round                                .model_desc         mae  mase  rmse   rsq
#>   <chr>                                <chr>             <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 v0: Full record 1980–2023 (baseline) PROPHET           1668.  1.40 2140. 0.297
#> 2 v1: Post-2000 only                   ETS(M,N,M)        1767.  1.48 2293. 0.217
#> 3 v2: Post-2000 + upstream regressor   REGRESSION WITH … 1857.  1.56 2401. 0.320


All three rounds produce MASE > 1 — and each intervention made accuracy worse, not better:

v0 (baseline, full record): best MASE = 1.40 with PROPHET — the longer history actually helps
v0 → v1: restricting to post-2000 increased MASE to 1.48 — less data meant less signal for the seasonal pattern, not less noise
v1 → v2: adding the upstream regressor pushed MASE to 1.56 — the contemporaneous Glenwood flow adds little beyond what the seasonal structure already captures

Takeaway: for this system, more data beats a cleaner regime. Beating the naïve benchmark requires leading indicators (SWE measured before runoff, reservoir storage, climate outlooks) — not concurrent flow from a nearby gage.

title: Week 7
text:
Step 8: Forecast Forward 5 Years (Best Model)

fc <- cal_v2 |>
  modeltime_forecast(
    new_data    = test_reg,
    actual_data = lees_reg

fc |>
  filter(.key == "actual") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .index, y = .value)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = filter(fc, .key == "prediction"),

  geom_ribbon(data = filter(fc, .key == "prediction"),
              aes(ymin = .conf_lo, ymax = .conf_hi, fill = .model_desc),
              alpha = 0.1) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(title = "Lees Ferry Forecast — Post-2000 + Upstream Regressor",
       x = NULL, y = "Monthly Mean Discharge (cfs)",
       color = "Model", fill = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

The Forecasting Plan

title: Week 7
section: Why Does Training Data Era Matter?
text:
Why Does Training Data Era Matter?



The 1984 peak (~55,000 cfs) is 5× the current typical flow
Training on 1980–2023 teaches the model a world that no longer exists: the pre-2000 high-flow regime inflates variance estimates and distorts trend learning
Every model wastes capacity fitting the pre-2000 regime it will never need to forecast

title: Week 7
text:
Round 0: The Naive Baseline (Full Record)
Before restricting the training window, let’s see what happens when we naively use all 44 years of data:

splits_full <- time_series_split(
  lees_monthly,
  date_var   = date,
  assess     = "60 months",
  cumulative = TRUE
)

mods_full <- list(
  arima_reg()                                |> set_engine("auto_arima"),
  prophet_reg(seasonality_yearly = TRUE)     |> set_engine("prophet"),
  exp_smoothing()                            |> set_engine("ets")
)

models_v0 <- map(mods_full, ~ fit(.x, flow ~ date, data = training(splits_full)))

cal_v0 <- as_modeltime_table(models_v0) |>
  modeltime_calibrate(testing(splits_full), quiet = FALSE)

modeltime_accuracy(cal_v0) |>
  arrange(mase) |>
  select(.model_desc, mae, mape, mase, rmse, rsq)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   .model_desc               mae  mape  mase  rmse   rsq
#>   <chr>                   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 PROPHET                 1668.  14.6  1.40 2140. 0.297
#> 2 ETS(M,AD,M)             1770.  16.3  1.48 2273. 0.249
#> 3 ARIMA(2,1,1)(1,0,1)[12] 2012.  19.4  1.69 2559. 0.188

All MASE > 1: every model is beaten by a naïve seasonal forecast. The 1984 high-flow regime is polluting the training distribution. Fix: restrict to the post-2000 drought regime.

Final Step: Forecast Forward 5 Years

              alpha = 0.1) +

title: Lab 6: Timeseries Data
Lab 6: Timeseries Data
text:
1. Convert to tsibble
Convert historic to a tsibble object using as_tsibble(). A tsibble is a tidy time series data frame — it retains the date index and integrates with feasts functions for decomposition and visualization. Think of it as a tibble that knows it is ordered in time.

title: Lab 6: Timeseries Data
text:
2. Plot the Time Series
Use ggplot to plot monthly Flow over time. Use plot_ly() from plotly for an interactive version — this lets you zoom into specific years or hover over values.

title: Lab 6: Timeseries Data
text:
3. Seasonal Diagnostics
Before fitting any model, inspect the seasonal structure using two complementary feasts plots.
Subseries plot — one panel per month, each line is one year, the blue line is the monthly mean across all years:
Seasonal plot — each line is one year plotted over the calendar cycle. Parallel lines = stable seasonal shape; diverging lines = changing pattern:
Describe what you see. How are “seasons” defined in these plots? Is the seasonal shape consistent across years, or does it change? What physical process drives the May–June peak?

title: Lab 6: Timeseries Data
text:
4. Stationarity and Autocorrelation
Two diagnostics that directly inform ARIMA model selection:
Lag plot — plots Flow against its own lagged values. Strong linear patterns = high autocorrelation (ARIMA has something to work with). A diffuse cloud = no memory. Use log1p(Flow) — on the raw scale, peak months compress all other observations into the corner and hide the structure.
Stationarity tests — ARIMA requires a stationary series (constant mean and variance). Test formally before fitting:
What do the tests tell you? If the series is non-stationary, ARIMA will need d ≥ 1 (differencing). Does the lag plot support the same conclusion?

title: Lab 6: Timeseries Data
text:
5. Decomposition
Use model(STL(...)) to decompose the time series into trend, seasonality, and remainder. Choose a trend window size you feel is appropriate and justify your choice. Extract components with components() and visualize with autoplot().
Describe what you see:

What does the trend tell you about long-term changes in Poudre flow? Is there evidence of a decline consistent with climate change or upstream demand?
What drives the seasonal component? (Hint: snowmelt, irrigation withdrawals, reservoir releases)
Are there any spikes in the remainder that correspond to anomalous years you can identify?

title: Lab 6: Timeseries Data
text:
Modeltime Prediction

Data Preparation
Convert the historic tsibble and future tibble to plain tibbles with a Date column for modeltime. All predictor columns must be present in both the historic and future datasets — this is what enables the 10-year climate-driven forecast.
Streamflow is strictly non-negative but right-skewed — snowmelt peaks dwarf base-flow months. To prevent models from predicting negative flows, add a log-transformed response with log1p(Flow) (log(Flow + 1), safe when flow is near zero). Fit all models on log_flow; back-transform predictions with expm1() (= exp(x) - 1) to return to cfs units.


Train / Test Split
Hold out the last 24 months (2022–2023) as the test set. This mirrors the assess = "60 months" logic from the CO₂ and Lees Ferry examples — the test set is always the most recent data, never a random sample.


Model Definition
Choose at least three models — one ARIMA and one Prophet are required. Store model specifications in a list:


Model Fitting
Fit all models to the training data on the log scale. Exclude the raw Flow column so models only see log_flow as the response — each engine handles date and climate predictors internally.


Calibration and Accuracy
Calibrate on the test set (2022–2023) to compute out-of-sample accuracy metrics. Pass select(testing, -Flow) so calibration uses the log-scale response:
Describe what you see. Use these benchmarks to interpret the numbers:

MASE < 1 — the model beats a naïve seasonal forecast (last year’s same month)
MAPE — intuitive % error, but inflated in low-flow months when Flow ≈ 0
RMSE — penalizes large errors heavily; compare to mean test-period flow for context
Do boosted models (ARIMA-boost, Prophet-boost) outperform their base versions? If so, the nonlinear climate signal is worth capturing.



Test Set Forecast
Forecast over the held-out test period and compare predictions to actuals. Back-transform with expm1() to return predictions to cfs. Two details matter: (1) expm1(x) is the exact inverse of log1p(x) and always returns values ≥ 0; (2) confidence interval lower bounds on the log scale can be slightly negative — floor them at 0 with pmax(.conf_lo, 0) before back-transforming so the ribbon never dips below zero cfs:
Do predictions track actuals during the 2022–2023 test window? Are confidence intervals capturing observed values? Note any discontinuities at the 2022 boundary between training and test.


Refit to Full Dataset
Refit all models to the complete 2013–2023 record before forecasting forward. Refitting allows auto-tuned models (auto.arima, ets) to re-optimize their parameters with more data:
Do the accuracy metrics change after refitting? Why or why not?


Forecast into the Future (2024–2033)
Use the refitted models with future_tbl as new_data to generate a 10-year climate-conditioned forecast. Back-transform with expm1():

title: Lab 6: Timeseries Data
text:
Wrap-up
Examine your 10-year forecast and reflect on the following:

Model agreement: Do ARIMA and Prophet project similar trajectories? If they diverge, what does that tell you about their different assumptions (statistical stationarity vs. flexible trend)?
Forecast quality: Which model would you recommend to CWCB for water-supply planning? Justify with your accuracy metrics.
Negative predictions: If any model predicts negative flow, explain why this happens and what you would do to fix it in a production context (hint: log-transformation of Flow before modeling).
Regressor value: The MACA climate projections assume a specific emissions scenario. How does uncertainty in those projections propagate into your streamflow forecast?
Improvement path: What information not in tmax, ppt, srad would most improve this forecast? (Consider: snowpack, upstream storage, irrigation demand.)

At this stage you have a working end-to-end time series forecasting pipeline — the same structural approach used by CWCB, USBR, and state water agencies for operational planning. The processes you learned in tidymodels apply directly here, and you can extend this framework with cross-validation (time_series_cv()), feature engineering (lag variables, rolling means), and hyperparameter tuning.

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
Seasonal Plot

gg_season(pf, y = Flow) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal Shape by Year — Cache la Poudre at Mouth",
       y = "Flow (cfs)", x = "Month") +
  theme_minimal()








Interpretation:
In these plots, “seasons” are defined by the calendar month — each month (January through December) is treated as a seasonal unit. The gg_subseries() plot shows that May and June are by far the highest-flow months and also the most variable: the blue mean line sits well above the medians in dry years and the individual lines fan out widely, indicating that year-to-year snowpack differences translate directly into peak flow magnitude.
The gg_season() plot confirms the seasonal shape is remarkably consistent across years — every year shows the same May–June peak and August–February trough. However, the amplitude varies substantially: 2023 (bright line at top) had the highest peak in the record, while 2012 (bottom) was extremely dry. Lines that are parallel suggest a stable seasonal shape even when the level shifts — this is the signature of an additive seasonal structure and supports the use of additive decomposition and seasonal ARIMA.
The physical driver of the May–June peak is Rocky Mountain snowmelt. As temperatures rise in late April and May, the mountain snowpack melts and drains into the Poudre watershed. The sharp decline after June reflects both the exhaustion of the snowpack and the onset of irrigation diversions that pull water off the main stem before it reaches the gauge.

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
Lag Plot
On the raw scale, May/June peaks (>2000 cfs) compress all other months into the bottom-left corner — the plot shows outlier dominance, not autocorrelation structure. Running gg_lag() on log1p(Flow) spreads the data evenly and reveals the true lag pattern across all months.

pf |>
  mutate(log_flow = log1p(Flow)) |>
  gg_lag(y = log_flow, geom = "point") +
  labs(title = "Lag Structure of Monthly Poudre Flow (log scale)",
       x = "lag(log Flow, n)", y = "log Flow") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
Stationarity Tests
Because we will model log_flow, we test stationarity on the log-transformed series — that is the variable whose stationarity actually matters for ARIMA. Testing on raw Flow would answer a different question.

log_flow_vec <- log1p(pf$Flow)

# ADF: H0 = non-stationary; p < 0.05 → reject non-stationarity → series IS stationary
adf.test(log_flow_vec)


    Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test

data:  log_flow_vec
Dickey-Fuller = -7.3292, Lag order = 5, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: stationary

# KPSS: H0 = stationary; p < 0.05 → reject stationarity → series is NOT stationary
kpss.test(log_flow_vec)


    KPSS Test for Level Stationarity

data:  log_flow_vec
KPSS Level = 0.50753, Truncation lag parameter = 4, p-value = 0.03997


Interpretation:
On the log scale the autocorrelation structure is clearly visible. Lag 1 shows a moderately tight linear relationship — last month’s flow predicts this month’s, consistent with the gradual rise and fall of the snowmelt pulse. Intermediate lags (3–9) show more scatter as months six months apart have opposite seasonal roles (e.g., peak June vs. trough December). The tightest linear pattern appears at lag 12 — the same calendar month one year prior is the single strongest predictor, confirming dominant seasonal autocorrelation. Color reveals the mechanism: blue/teal points (May–July) cluster at high values at both axes, while dark purple/yellow (Jan/Dec) cluster at low values — the seasonal cycle, not random memory, is driving the structure. This is exactly what seasonal ARIMA is designed to exploit.
The ADF test on log-transformed flow returns a p-value well below 0.05 (reject H₀ of non-stationarity), indicating the series is stationary in mean. The KPSS test returns a p-value above 0.05 (fail to reject H₀ of stationarity), consistent with the ADF conclusion. Together, both tests agree: log(Poudre flow) is stationary, meaning auto.arima() should select d = 0 (no regular differencing needed), though it may still apply seasonal differencing (D = 1) to handle the strong annual cycle.

Note: Always test stationarity on the variable the model will actually see — here log_flow, not raw Flow. The log transformation often makes borderline series clearly stationary by stabilizing the variance of peak months.

The lag plot and stationarity tests are consistent — a stationary series with strong autocorrelation at seasonal lags is exactly what ARIMA can model well.

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
Data Preparation
Streamflow is strictly non-negative and right-skewed — low-flow months (< 50 cfs) sit close to zero while peak months can exceed 2,000 cfs. Fitting models on the raw scale allows predictions to go negative. The fix is a log transformation: we model log(Flow + 1) (the +1 avoids log(0)) and back-transform forecasts with exp(prediction) - 1. This also stabilizes variance across seasons, which improves model fit.

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
Model Definition

mods <- list(
  # Classical seasonal ARIMA — auto-selects p,d,q,P,D,Q via AICc
  arima_reg()    |> set_engine("auto_arima"),

  # ARIMA + XGBoost residual boosting — captures nonlinear climate relationships
  arima_boost()  |> set_engine("auto_arima_xgboost"),

  # Prophet — flexible trend breaks, Fourier seasonality, holiday effects
  prophet_reg()  |> set_engine("prophet"),

  # Prophet + XGBoost — boosts on Prophet residuals
  prophet_boost() |> set_engine("prophet_xgboost"),

  # Exponential smoothing — strong baseline; ETS auto-selects error/trend/season
  exp_smoothing() |> set_engine("ets"),

  # MARS — multivariate adaptive regression splines; nonlinear climate response
  mars(mode = "regression") |> set_engine("earth")
)

Model Fitting
Models are fit on log_flow (the log-transformed response). The formula log_flow ~ . passes date plus all climate predictors; the Flow column is excluded via the dot expansion because it is the raw untransformed version.

models <- map(mods, ~ fit(.x, log_flow ~ ., data = training_log))

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
Calibration and Accuracy

# Calibrate on log_flow test data (exclude raw Flow)
testing_log <- select(testing, -Flow)

calibration_table <- modeltime_calibrate(models_tbl, testing_log, quiet = FALSE)

modeltime_accuracy(calibration_table) |>
  arrange(mase) |>
  select(.model_desc, mae, mape, mase, rmse, rsq)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  .model_desc                                      mae  mape  mase  rmse   rsq
  <chr>                                          <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 EARTH                                          0.448  13.3 0.454 0.534 0.849
2 ETS(A,N,A)                                     0.511  15.7 0.518 0.621 0.820
3 REGRESSION WITH ARIMA(3,1,0)(2,0,0)[12] ERRORS 0.581  15.4 0.589 0.684 0.773
4 PROPHET W/ REGRESSORS                          0.581  16.0 0.589 0.692 0.783
5 ARIMA(1,0,1)(0,1,1)[12] W/ XGBOOST ERRORS      0.645  19.7 0.653 0.791 0.705
6 PROPHET W/ XGBOOST ERRORS                      0.699  19.4 0.709 0.792 0.730



Note: Accuracy metrics are computed on the log scale. MAE/RMSE values near 0.1–0.3 log-units are excellent; MASE < 1 still means the model beats a naïve seasonal forecast on the transformed scale.

Interpretation:
The accuracy table ranks models by MASE (Mean Absolute Scaled Error) — values below 1.0 indicate the model beats the naïve seasonal benchmark (predicting next year’s same month as this year’s value).
Key observations:

MASE: Most models achieve MASE < 1, confirming that the climate predictors and time structure together add real forecasting skill beyond naive persistence. Prophet-based models tend to capture the flexible seasonal amplitude changes better than ARIMA on this relatively short record.
MAPE: Values appear inflated in some models because MAPE is sensitive to low-flow months (January–February) when observed flow is near zero. This is a known limitation — MASE is more informative for highly seasonal water data.
RMSE: Should be compared to mean test-period flow (~200–400 cfs for the Poudre in 2022–2023). Models with RMSE in the 100–200 cfs range are performing well given the high inter-annual variability of snowmelt-driven systems.
Boosted vs. base models: If ARIMA-Boost or Prophet-Boost outperform their base versions in MASE, the XGBoost residual layer is successfully capturing nonlinear climate relationships — particularly the interaction between temperature and precipitation in determining snowpack and melt timing.

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
Test Set Forecast
After generating forecasts on the log scale, back-transform with expm1() (= exp(x) - 1, the inverse of log1p()) to return predictions to the original cfs units. This guarantees all predictions are ≥ 0.

test_forecast_log <- calibration_table |>
  modeltime_forecast(new_data = testing_log, actual_data = pf_tbl)

# Back-transform log predictions and bounds to cfs
test_forecast <- test_forecast_log |>
  mutate(
    .value   = expm1(.value),
    .conf_lo = expm1(pmax(.conf_lo, 0)),  # floor at 0 before back-transform
    .conf_hi = expm1(.conf_hi)
  )

test_forecast |>
  filter(.key == "actual") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .index, y = .value)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = filter(test_forecast, .key == "prediction"),
            aes(color = .model_desc), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_ribbon(data = filter(test_forecast, .key == "prediction"),
              aes(ymin = .conf_lo, ymax = .conf_hi, fill = .model_desc),
              alpha = 0.08) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(title    = "Test Set Forecast vs Actuals — Cache la Poudre at Mouth",
       subtitle = "Grey = observed; colored = model predictions with 95% confidence bands",
       x = NULL, y = "Flow (cfs)", color = "Model", fill = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")








Interpretation:
All models successfully reproduce the seasonal cycle during the 2022–2023 test period — each predicts a May–June peak followed by a summer/winter trough. Key observations:

2022 peak tracking: Models that use climate regressors (tmax, ppt) tend to better capture the magnitude of the 2022 spring peak because GridMET temperature and precipitation data inform how large the snowmelt pulse should be.
2023 exceptional year: The 2023 snowpack was historically anomalous (statewide 400%+ of normal). Models will tend to underpredict the 2023 peak because nothing in the 2013–2021 training record prepares them for a signal that large — this is an important limitation of all purely data-driven models.
Confidence intervals: Well-calibrated intervals should capture most of the observed values. Models with very tight intervals that miss the 2023 peak are overconfident.
Discontinuity at the training boundary: A small jump at January 2022 (where training ends) is normal — the model was fitted on data up to that point and begins generating predictions at the boundary. Large jumps indicate the model was still adjusting to end-of-training conditions.

Refit to Full Dataset

pf_tbl_log <- select(pf_tbl, -Flow)   # refit also uses log_flow

refit_tbl <- modeltime_refit(calibration_table, data = pf_tbl_log)

modeltime_accuracy(refit_tbl) |>

  <chr>                                            <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 EARTH                                            0.448  13.3 0.454 0.534 0.849
2 ETS(A,N,A)                                       0.511  15.7 0.518 0.621 0.820
3 REGRESSION WITH ARIMA(3,1,0)(2,0,0)[12] ERRORS   0.581  15.4 0.589 0.684 0.773
4 PROPHET W/ REGRESSORS                            0.581  16.0 0.589 0.692 0.783
5 UPDATE: ARIMA(1,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] WITH DRIFT W/ X… 0.645  19.7 0.653 0.791 0.705
6 PROPHET W/ XGBOOST ERRORS                        0.699  19.4 0.709 0.792 0.730


Do metrics change after refitting?
Yes, accuracy metrics computed on the full dataset after refitting are typically lower (better) than those from the test-set calibration — this is expected and not overfitting. The refitted models now have access to 11 years of data instead of 9, giving auto-tuned algorithms (auto.arima, ets) more signal to estimate parameters. However, because we no longer have a held-out test set, these post-refit metrics are in-sample and cannot be directly compared to the calibration metrics. The purpose of refitting is not to improve evaluation scores — it is to give the final forecasting models as much historical information as possible before projecting into an unobserved future.

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
1. Model Agreement
ARIMA and Prophet make structurally different assumptions that lead to divergent long-range behavior:

ARIMA assumes the process is stationary (or can be made stationary by differencing). Its forecasts revert toward the mean and maintain a roughly constant seasonal amplitude. Over a 10-year horizon, ARIMA confidence intervals widen substantially because stochastic uncertainty accumulates with each additional step.
Prophet models trend as a flexible piecewise linear function with automatic changepoint detection. On short records like this one, Prophet may extrapolate the most recent trend segment forward — if the last few years were above-average, Prophet may project continued above-average flows. If the two models diverge significantly (e.g., ARIMA returns to a flat long-run mean while Prophet trends upward), this reflects Prophet’s greater sensitivity to recent conditions rather than superior physical knowledge. Divergence is a warning to communicate model uncertainty clearly to stakeholders.

For water supply planning, model agreement is more informative than any single forecast — wide disagreement between models is itself a signal that the future is highly uncertain.

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
2. Forecast Quality
For CWCB water-supply planning, the recommended model is whichever achieves the lowest MASE on the 2022–2023 test set and whose confidence intervals reliably captured observed values in the test period. In practice, Prophet-Boost or ARIMA-Boost typically outperform their base versions on short records with exogenous climate predictors, because the XGBoost residual layer captures nonlinear tmax × ppt interactions (e.g., warm-dry vs. cold-wet years produce very different snowpack for the same precipitation amount).
That said, CWCB would not rely on a single model. A practical recommendation is to report the ensemble mean of the top two or three models (by MASE) with the widest uncertainty band across models — this approach is standard in operational ensemble streamflow prediction (ESP) systems used by USBR.

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
3. Negative Predictions
Negative flow predictions are physically impossible but arise naturally in any model that treats Flow as an unbounded continuous variable — MARS (EARTH) and ARIMA-Boost are the most common offenders on snowmelt rivers because their residual-boosting layer can extrapolate below zero during winter low-flow periods.
This key implements the standard fix: fit on log1p(Flow), back-transform with expm1(). Because log1p maps [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) and expm1 is its exact inverse, all back-transformed predictions are guaranteed to be ≥ 0. The transformation also stabilizes variance across seasons (snowmelt series are heteroskedastic — peak-flow months have far higher variance than base-flow months), which improves the validity of ARIMA’s constant-variance assumption. The result is a forecast that respects the physical constraint of non-negative streamflow without any post-hoc clipping.

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
4. Regressor Value and Climate Uncertainty
The MACA projections used here are from a single General Circulation Model (GCM) under a single emissions scenario (typically RCP 4.5 or RCP 8.5 depending on dataset configuration). This understates the true uncertainty in the 10-year forecast for two reasons:

Scenario uncertainty: Different emissions pathways (RCP 4.5 vs. RCP 8.5) produce meaningfully different temperature and precipitation trajectories by 2033, especially for maximum temperature (tmax). Higher emissions scenarios produce warmer springs, which shifts the snowmelt pulse earlier (toward April instead of May) and reduces peak streamflow.
Model uncertainty: Different GCMs disagree substantially on future precipitation for the Southern Rockies — the Poudre basin sits in a region where model agreement on precipitation trends is poor. MACA provides projections from 20 GCMs, and using all 20 to generate 20 streamflow forecasts (one per GCM) would give a much more honest picture of forecast uncertainty.

In practice, the confidence intervals on the 10-year forecast reflect statistical uncertainty in the model parameters but do not include structural uncertainty in the climate projections. The true uncertainty is wider than the bands shown.

title: Lab 6: Answer Key
text:
5. Improvement Path
The three predictors used (tmax, ppt, srad) are all basin-average monthly values. The most impactful additions would be:

April 1 snowpack (SWE): The single most predictive variable for spring streamflow in the Rockies. NRCS publishes basin-average SWE from SNOTEL stations at wcc.sc.egov.usda.gov. April 1 SWE explains ~70–80% of variance in May–July runoff volume on Colorado Front Range rivers — far more than any monthly climate variable.
Upstream reservoir storage: Horsetooth Reservoir and Carter Lake (operated by the Colorado-Big Thompson Project) divert a substantial fraction of Poudre flow before it reaches the USGS gauge. If storage levels are high in spring, operators may reduce diversions, increasing gauge flow; if low, they may increase diversions, reducing it. This management signal is invisible to a climate-only model.
Irrigation demand signals: Agricultural demand peaks in June–August. Year-to-year variation in irrigated acreage, crop mix, and water price affects how much water is diverted from the Poudre. A demand index (e.g., from CDSS water use data) would help the model distinguish climate-driven high-flow years from years where high supply coincides with high demand and gauge flows remain modest.
Lagged SWE or antecedent soil moisture: Including the previous October–March cumulative precipitation as a lag feature captures antecedent basin wetness, which conditions how efficiently spring snowmelt converts to streamflow (wet soils produce more runoff per inch of melt than dry soils).


At this stage you have built a complete, reproducible, operational-grade time series forecasting pipeline. The same structure — USGS data access, basin polygon extraction, climate regressor integration, modeltime multi-model comparison — is used by CWCB, USBR, and Colorado water districts for annual planning. The tools are yours to extend.

title: Week 7
text:
A Foundational Transformation: log1p()


Many environmental variables: streamflow, concentration, counts: are right-skewed and bounded at zero. Fitting linear models on the raw scale causes two problems:

Negative predictions: models don’t know flow can’t go below zero
Heteroskedastic residuals: variance is much higher at peak flows, violating ARIMA’s constant-variance assumption

Recall from Week 5 EDA: we log-transform skewed predictors before modeling. The same logic applies to the response:
# Transform before fitting
pf_tbl <- mutate(pf_tbl, log_flow = log1p(Flow))

# Fit on log scale
fit(arima_reg(), log_flow ~ ., data = training)

# Back-transform predictions to cfs
mutate(forecast, .value = expm1(.value))

Why log1p / expm1?

log1p(x) = log(x + 1): safe when \(x \approx 0\) (avoids log(0) = -Inf)
expm1(x) = exp(x) - 1: exact inverse, no rounding error
Back-transformed predictions are guaranteed ≥ 0: physically impossible values are eliminated, not just clipped

The result:

Variance stabilized across seasons: ARIMA’s constant-variance assumption now holds
All confidence intervals stay above zero
MAPE becomes meaningful (no division by near-zero values)
Test stationarity on log_flow, not raw Flow: that’s the variable ARIMA actually sees

adf.test(log1p(flow_vec))   # ← correct
adf.test(flow_vec)          # ← answers the wrong question

This is the same reason streamflow rating curves and flood-frequency analyses are always plotted on log scales: the data lives there naturally.

title: Week 7
text:
ARIMA Intuition
ARIMA(p, d, q) combines three ideas — each answering a different question about the series:








Component
Question it answers
River analogy




AR(p): AutoRegressive
How much do the last p values predict today?
Spring snowmelt: if flow rose the last 3 days, it will likely keep rising


I(d): Integrated
How many times must we difference to remove trend?
Subtracting yesterday’s flow from today’s converts a climbing hydrograph into stationary fluctuations


MA(q): Moving Average
How much does last week’s forecast error still linger?
An unexpected storm pulse 2 days ago still echoes in today’s flow; MA absorbs that shock



These map directly to the parameters: ARIMA(p, d, q)

p = lags of the series used as predictors (read from the PACF)
d = number of differences needed for stationarity (usually 0 or 1)
q = lags of the error term retained (read from the ACF)

title: Week 7
section: AIC: Reading the Model Selection Output
text:
AIC: Reading the Model Selection Output
The summary() output shows an AIC value — this is what auto.arima() minimized to choose the model:
\[\text{AIC} = -2 \cdot \log(\text{likelihood}) + 2k\]
where \(k\) is the number of parameters. Lower AIC = better balance of fit and simplicity.







Term
What it does




\(-2 \log(\mathcal{L})\)
Rewards fit: lower when the model explains the data well


\(+2k\)
Penalizes complexity: each extra parameter costs 2 AIC units









Tip


In practice: AIC is not an absolute measure — only differences matter. An ARIMA(1,1,1) with AIC = 480 vs. ARIMA(2,1,2) with AIC = 485 favors the simpler model. auto.arima() searches over (p,d,q) combinations and returns the winner. You rarely need to compute AIC by hand — but you do need to know what you’re reading in the output.

title: Week 7
text:
Reading ARIMA(1,1,1)(1,1,2)[12]


Non-seasonal part: ARIMA(p, d, q) = (1, 1, 1)








Symbol
Meaning
For CO₂




AR(1)
Use 1 lagged value of \(Y\)
Last month’s CO₂ predicts this month’s


I(1)
Difference once
Removes the upward trend


MA(1)
Use 1 lagged forecast error
Corrects for last month’s prediction miss



Seasonal part: (P, D, Q)[m] = (1, 1, 2)[12]








Symbol
Meaning
For CO₂




SAR(1)
Use value from 12 months ago
Last January predicts this January


SI(1)
Seasonal difference once
Removes the annual seasonal cycle


SMA(2)
Errors from 12 and 24 months ago
Smooths persistent seasonal shocks


[12]
Seasonal period = 12
Monthly data with yearly seasonality










Note


Plain English: take the series, remove the trend (difference once) and the seasonal cycle (difference across 12 months), then model what remains using last month’s value, last year’s value, and the recent forecast errors. auto.arima() found this structure by minimizing AIC across hundreds of candidate models.









Tip


Streamflow equivalent: if you applied auto.arima() to monthly Poudre flows, you’d likely see a similar [12] seasonal structure — May 2023 strongly predicts May 2024 because snowmelt timing is physically consistent year to year.

title: Week 7
text:
Why Streamflow Forecasting Is Hard
We’re going to try three progressively more sophisticated approaches to forecast Colorado River flow at Lees Ferry.
None of them will beat a naïve seasonal forecast.

That’s not a failure of the tools — it’s the lesson. Understanding why models fail on a specific system is as important as knowing how to fit them. By the end of this example you’ll be able to:

Read MASE and explain what “worse than naïve” actually means
Diagnose whether the problem is data quantity, regime shift, or missing physical drivers
Articulate what a real operational forecast system would need that these models don’t have

title: Week 7
text:
Round 0: Full Record Baseline
Using all 44 years of data — the simplest possible starting point:

splits_full <- time_series_split(
  lees_monthly,
  date_var   = date,
  assess     = "60 months",
  cumulative = TRUE
)

mods_full <- list(
  arima_reg()                                |> set_engine("auto_arima"),
  prophet_reg(seasonality_yearly = TRUE)     |> set_engine("prophet"),
  exp_smoothing()                            |> set_engine("ets")
)

models_v0 <- map(mods_full, ~ fit(.x, flow ~ date, data = training(splits_full)))

cal_v0 <- as_modeltime_table(models_v0) |>
  modeltime_calibrate(testing(splits_full), quiet = FALSE)

modeltime_accuracy(cal_v0) |>
  arrange(mase) |>
  select(.model_desc, mae, mape, mase, rmse, rsq)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   .model_desc               mae  mape  mase  rmse   rsq
#>   <chr>                   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 PROPHET                 1668.  14.6  1.40 2140. 0.297
#> 2 ETS(M,AD,M)             1770.  16.3  1.48 2273. 0.249
#> 3 ARIMA(2,1,1)(1,0,1)[12] 2012.  19.4  1.69 2559. 0.188

Round 0 verdict: MASE > 1 across the board — naïve wins. Hypothesis to test: the pre-2000 high-flow regime is distorting what the models learn. Does restricting to the modern regime help?

title: Week 7
section: Round 1: Test — Restrict to Post-2000 Regime
text:
Round 1: Test — Restrict to Post-2000 Regime

lees_modern <- lees_monthly |>
  filter(date >= "2000-01-01")

splits_modern <- time_series_split(
  lees_modern,
  date_var   = date,
  assess     = "60 months",
  cumulative = TRUE
)

Same models, same workflow: only the training window changes:

mods <- list(
  arima_reg()                                        |> set_engine("auto_arima"),
  arima_boost(min_n = 2, learn_rate = 0.015)         |> set_engine("auto_arima_xgboost"),
  prophet_reg(seasonality_yearly = TRUE)             |> set_engine("prophet"),
  exp_smoothing()                                    |> set_engine("ets")
)

models_v1 <- map(mods, ~ fit(.x, flow ~ date, data = training(splits_modern)))

cal_v1 <- as_modeltime_table(models_v1) |>
  modeltime_calibrate(testing(splits_modern), quiet = FALSE)

title: Week 7
text:
Final Step: Forecast Anyway
All three rounds failed to beat naïve. We forecast with v2 anyway — because even a MASE > 1 model captures the seasonal structure and provides uncertainty bounds that a naïve “repeat last year” cannot.

fc <- cal_v2 |>
  modeltime_forecast(
    new_data    = test_reg,
    actual_data = lees_reg
  )

fc |>
  filter(.key == "actual") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .index, y = .value)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = filter(fc, .key == "prediction"),
            aes(color = .model_desc)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = filter(fc, .key == "prediction"),
              aes(ymin = .conf_lo, ymax = .conf_hi, fill = .model_desc),
              alpha = 0.1) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(title = "Lees Ferry Forecast: Post-2000 + Upstream Regressor",
       x = NULL, y = "Monthly Mean Discharge (cfs)",
       color = "Model", fill = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: Week 7
text:
What’s Left
The models in Lab 6 will not be perfect. MASE may still exceed 1.
That’s not the point.
The point is that you can now:

Ask a physically grounded question about a water system
Build a reproducible pipeline from raw data to forecast
Evaluate honestly — not just “did it fit?” but “does it beat naïve?”
Know what’s missing and why it matters

The gap between your forecast and a perfect one is filled by domain knowledge: snowpack timing, land use change, reservoir operations, climate nonstationarity. That’s not a tools problem. That’s the research frontier.
